title: Hello World: Starting a Career in Java Backend Engineering
content:
Every engineer remembers their first System.out.println("Hello, World!");. Mine was the moment I decided backend engineering was where I wanted to build my career — not just write code, but design systems that handle real users, real load, and real failures.

This blog is my engineering log. I will write about things I build, problems I debug in production, and patterns I learn from reading other engineers' work. Less theory, more real decisions and their consequences.

What I Am Building Right Now

My current focus project is Nexus — a live multiplayer game platform built with Java 17, Spring Boot 3, WebSocket (STOMP/SockJS), and PostgreSQL. It has real users, real concurrent sessions, and real production bugs that I have had to debug at 11pm.

Some things I have shipped so far:

  • Replaced JavaMailSender (SMTP port 587, blocked by Railway's firewall) with Resend HTTP API after diagnosing a 2-minute silent timeout in production.
  • Fixed a JPQL inner-class syntax bug — User$UserStatus.OFFLINE — that crashed a scheduled task every 10 seconds and silently rejected all game moves.
  • Closed an XSS surface in the lobby player list by replacing inline onclick username interpolation with data-target attributes and addEventListener.

These are not textbook problems. They are production problems, and solving them taught me more than any course did.

Why Remote Engineering

Remote work is not about flexibility for me — it is about access to the kind of work I want to do. The most interesting backend problems are not concentrated in one city. The teams working on distributed systems, real-time communication, and open-source infrastructure are global. I want to be part of that.

What Is Next

I am actively working on migrating Nexus from Railway (trial expired) to Oracle Cloud Always Free, setting up GitHub Actions CI/CD, and adding the Human vs AI game mode. I will write about each of these as they ship.

If you are a recruiter, a fellow Java engineer, or someone who found this through a search for Spring Boot WebSocket debugging — welcome. I hope something here is useful.

title: Why Your Spring Boot Emails Hang for 2 Minutes on Railway
content:
I spent two days debugging a registration flow where users were saved to the database but never received an activation email. The backend returned 200 OK. Resend's dashboard showed zero activity. The logs showed nothing.

The root cause: Railway's infrastructure blocks outbound port 587. JavaMailSender opens a TCP socket to smtp.resend.com:587, waits for a connection that never arrives, times out after ~2 minutes, and then the catch block swallows the exception entirely.

How I Diagnosed It

The first clue was the Railway HTTP logs. POST /api/users/register was taking exactly 2 minutes and 15 seconds. A normal register should take under 200ms. Something was blocking the thread.

The second clue was Resend's dashboard showing zero API calls — which meant the request was never leaving the server, not being rejected by Resend.

Port 587 (SMTP STARTTLS) is commonly blocked by cloud platforms because it is a spam vector. Port 465 (SMTP SSL) is sometimes allowed. Port 443 (HTTPS) is never blocked.

The Fix

Replace JavaMailSender entirely with a direct HTTP call to Resend's REST API on port 443.

HttpHeaders headers = new HttpHeaders();
headers.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON);
headers.setBearerAuth(resendApiKey);

Map<String, Object> body = new HashMap<>();
body.put("from",    "noreply@nexusgame.space");
body.put("to",      List.of(toEmail));
body.put("subject", "Activate Your Account");
body.put("html",    htmlContent);

restTemplate.postForEntity(
    "https://api.resend.com/emails",
    new HttpEntity<>(body, headers),
    String.class
);

Delivery time went from a 2-minute timeout to under 1 second. No SMTP configuration needed. No port issues.

Lessons

  • Never swallow exceptions in email send methods — at minimum, log the full stack trace so you can find the problem later.
  • Always save to the database before sending email, never after. If email fails, the user record still exists and you can resend.
  • When diagnosing slow API endpoints, check external calls first. A 2-minute response time is almost always a network timeout, not a CPU or DB issue.

title: The JPQL Bug That Crashed My Game Every 10 Seconds
content:
For a week, active game sessions in Nexus would randomly reject player moves. The board would appear ready, both players could see it, but clicking a cell did nothing. No error in the browser. The server logs showed a scheduled task throwing an exception every 10 seconds.

The Stack Trace

Buried in the logs was this:

org.hibernate.query.SemanticException: Could not interpret path expression 
'com.vk.gaming.nexus.entity.User$UserStatus.OFFLINE'

The $ character is the JVM bytecode separator for inner classes — User$UserStatus is how the compiled class file is named on disk. JPQL uses Java source-level syntax where inner classes use . not $. Hibernate 6 is stricter about this than Hibernate 5 was.

The Broken Query

@Query("""
    UPDATE User u 
    SET u.status = com.vk.gaming.nexus.entity.User$UserStatus.OFFLINE
    WHERE u.lastSeen < :cutoff 
    AND u.status <> com.vk.gaming.nexus.entity.User$UserStatus.OFFLINE
""")
int markInactiveUsersOffline(@Param("cutoff") long cutoff);

The Fix

Pass the enum value as a named parameter instead of embedding it in the JPQL string. This is the correct approach regardless of Hibernate version.

@Query("""
    UPDATE User u
    SET u.status = :offline
    WHERE u.lastSeen < :cutoff
    AND u.status <> :offline
""")
int markInactiveUsersOffline(
    @Param("cutoff") long cutoff,
    @Param("offline") User.UserStatus offline
);

The caller passes User.UserStatus.OFFLINE as an argument. Hibernate serialises it correctly for the target database dialect.

Why It Affected Game Moves

The scheduled task ran every 10 seconds via @Scheduled(fixedRate = 10000). When it threw an exception, it rolled back its transaction. In some transaction isolation configurations, this caused the connection pool to enter an inconsistent state that rejected the next few operations — including game move saves. The timing appeared random from the player's perspective.

The fix to the JPQL query stopped the scheduled task from throwing, which stopped the move rejection entirely.

title: Building Real-Time Multiplayer with Spring Boot WebSocket and STOMP
content:
WebSocket gives you a persistent bidirectional connection between client and server. STOMP (Simple Text Oriented Message Protocol) runs on top of WebSocket and gives you topics, subscriptions, and message routing — the things you actually need to build a multiplayer game.

Here is how the Nexus game architecture works end to end.

Server Configuration

@Configuration
@EnableWebSocketMessageBroker
public class WebSocketConfig implements WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void configureMessageBroker(MessageBrokerRegistry config) {
        config.enableSimpleBroker("/topic");
        config.setApplicationDestinationPrefixes("/app");
    }

    @Override
    public void registerStompEndpoints(StompEndpointRegistry registry) {
        registry.addEndpoint("/game-websocket")
                .setAllowedOriginPatterns("*")
                .withSockJS();
    }
}

Messages sent to /app/something are routed to @MessageMapping methods. Messages sent to /topic/something are broadcast to all subscribers of that topic.

The Challenge Flow

When Player A challenges Player B:

  1. Client sends to /app/challenge with {sender, receiver, roomId}
  2. Server receives in @MessageMapping("/challenge")
  3. Server broadcasts to /topic/challenges/{receiver}
  4. Player B's client, subscribed to their personal channel, receives the challenge

This is the key insight: each player has a private topic /topic/challenges/{username}. Game moves go to a shared room topic /topic/game/{roomId} that both players subscribe to.

One Bug That Took Hours to Find

The handleGameMove method was missing @Payload:

// Broken — Spring fails to deserialise the body
@MessageMapping("/move/{roomId}")
public void handleGameMove(@DestinationVariable String roomId, GameMove move) {}

// Fixed
@MessageMapping("/move/{roomId}")
public void handleGameMove(@DestinationVariable String roomId, @Payload GameMove move) {}

When @DestinationVariable is present alongside a body parameter, Spring WebSocket requires @Payload explicitly. Without it, Jackson fails to bind the JSON body and move.getRoomId() returns null, causing every move to be silently rejected.

State Recovery After Restart

All game state (who is X, who is O, whose turn) lives in in-memory ConcurrentHashMap instances. A server restart wipes them. The fix is recoverGameStateFromDB — when a move arrives for a room with no in-memory state, the server rebuilds it from the move history in PostgreSQL.

title: Linux Commands Every Java Developer Should Know
content:
If you deploy Java applications to any Linux server — and you will — these commands will save you hours. I use all of these regularly when working with Nexus on Ubuntu.

Process Management

# See if your Spring Boot app is running
ps aux | grep java

# Kill a process by port (useful when port 8080 is already in use)
sudo lsof -t -i:8080 | xargs kill -9

# Check port usage
ss -tlnp | grep 8080

Logs

# Follow live Spring Boot logs from systemd
sudo journalctl -u nexus -f

# Last 100 lines
sudo journalctl -u nexus -n 100

# Logs since a specific time
sudo journalctl -u nexus --since "2026-04-08 10:00"

File and Deployment

# Copy a JAR from local machine to server
scp -i ~/.ssh/key.pem app.jar ubuntu@server_ip:/opt/app/

# Check disk space (important on free-tier VMs)
df -h

# Check available memory
free -h

Systemd Service Commands

# Start / stop / restart
sudo systemctl start nexus
sudo systemctl stop nexus
sudo systemctl restart nexus

# Check status
sudo systemctl status nexus

# Enable on boot
sudo systemctl enable nexus

The most useful of these for daily Java development is journalctl -f. Watching live logs while testing an API endpoint is faster than any IDE output window.

title: The 10 DSA Patterns That Cover 80% of Interview Problems
content:
After solving 150+ problems in Java, I noticed that most problems fall into a small number of patterns. Recognising the pattern is faster than solving each problem from scratch.

1. Two Pointers

Use when the input is sorted or you need to find pairs. One pointer starts at each end and they move toward each other.

// Find pair with target sum in sorted array
int left = 0, right = nums.length - 1;
while (left < right) {
    int sum = nums[left] + nums[right];
    if (sum == target) return new int[]{left, right};
    else if (sum < target) left++;
    else right--;
}

2. Sliding Window

Use for contiguous subarray/substring problems. Expand the right pointer, shrink from left when a condition is violated.

3. Fast and Slow Pointers

Use for cycle detection in linked lists. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually catch the slow pointer.

4. BFS on a Graph or Grid

Use when you need the shortest path or need to explore level by level. Always use a visited set to avoid revisiting nodes.

Queue<int[]> queue = new LinkedList<>();
Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>();
queue.offer(start);
while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int[] curr = queue.poll();
    // process curr
    for (int[] neighbor : getNeighbors(curr)) {
        String key = neighbor[0] + "," + neighbor[1];
        if (!visited.contains(key)) {
            visited.add(key);
            queue.offer(neighbor);
        }
    }
}

5. DFS with Backtracking

Use for permutations, combinations, and path-finding problems. Choose, explore, then unchoose.

6. Dynamic Programming — 1D

Use when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Start with recursion, add memoisation, then convert to bottom-up tabulation.

7. Dynamic Programming — 2D

Common for grid paths, edit distance, and knapsack problems. Build a table where dp[i][j] represents the answer for a subproblem of size i×j.

8. Binary Search

Not just for sorted arrays. Any problem where the search space can be halved — finding the minimum valid value, peak element, or rotated array search — is a binary search problem.

9. Heap / Priority Queue

Use for top-K problems and problems where you repeatedly need the minimum or maximum. Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default.

10. Monotonic Stack

Use for next greater element, largest rectangle, and span problems. Maintain a stack that is always sorted by pushing and popping as needed.

The goal is not to memorise solutions — it is to recognise which pattern applies in the first 60 seconds of reading a problem. That recognition is what changes your interview performance.
